content: Public procurement processes must ensure that potential suppliers are provided with precise technical information and detailed specifications for the products to be procured. Open tenders are often announced through advertisements in newspapers, international journals, or online platforms to encourage competition and enable procurement entities to secure pesticides at the most competitive prices. The tender documents should include technical specifications and other requirements that define the commercial and logistical framework for procurement. These may include Incoterms (e.g., free carrier to the nearest main sea or airport), ordering procedures, applicable terms and conditions for supplier selection, submission deadlines for bids (ensuring sufficient time to allow fair competition), and schedules for orders and delivery. Bidders should be informed of any anticipated delays, such as if the pesticides have not yet been authorized for use in the destination country. The documents should also outline procedures for awarding tenders, any special conditions (e.g., preference for WHO-recommended products), and requests for statements regarding the supplier’s administrative and legal status, as well as their relationship to the product. A standardized proposal form should be included, detailing delivery times, expected delivery dates, gross weight of the order, personnel involved, contact details, and a total cost quotation, including any discounts. Additional information in the tender documents should specify the name and address of the procurement entity and the delivery location for the goods. If registration or authorization for importing the pesticide or long-lasting insecticidal nets (LNs) in the country of use is a prerequisite for procurement, this information must be included in the tender specifications. Administrative requirements, such as insurance, advance payment percentages, payment schedules, interest for payment delays, and performance bonds for satisfactory contract completion, may also be included. The procurement of high-quality pesticides begins with defining the correct specifications for their intended purpose. Personnel responsible for drafting these specifications must possess the necessary expertise and experience. Incomplete or inappropriate specifications in tenders and procurement documents can lead to significant issues with pesticide use. Specifications should include the formulation type (e.g., wettable powder, emulsifiable concentrate, suspension concentrate), relevant chemical and physical properties with acceptable limits, maximum permissible levels of impurities, storage stability requirements under various temperature conditions, and compliance with WHO specifications and recommendations, if applicable. For LNs, specifications should include details such as the identity and content of active ingredients, fiber and filament type, denier, impregnation technology, color, size, shape, active ingredient retention index, seam stitching (number and location), netting mesh size and shape, dimensional stability to washing, bursting strength, and storage stability at elevated temperatures. WHO-recommended LNs are identified by specific WHO specifications, and tenders should reference these specifications to ensure eligibility. Packaging requirements should also be specified in the tender documents, including the type, material thickness, size, and durability suitable for local use and climatic conditions. Packaging must comply with United Nations recommendations for the transport of dangerous goods. Proper packaging size facilitates field application and minimizes risks of spillage, inaccurate dosing, and exposure during application. While bulk purchasing may be economical, it should be weighed against the risks associated with handling and application. LNs should be individually packed in sealed plastic bags strong enough to prevent damage during transit. Labels should be printed on the bag or inserted in a transparent plastic bag inside. Rectangular nets should typically have six hanging loops made of reinforced fabric or netting material, while conical nets should include a non-rusting ring. To reduce transport costs, manufacturers are encouraged to bale LNs in quantities of 50, 40, or 25 per bale, with secondary outer packaging for protection and proper strapping and labeling. Tenderers must provide evidence that the packaging meets national requirements or, in their absence, is robust enough to prevent leakage and breakage during shipment and local transport. Labeling requirements are critical to ensure proper pesticide use, prevent misuse, and avoid incidents such as poisoning and environmental contamination. Tender documents must explicitly define labeling requirements, which should comply with national regulations, including language specifications, and align with the International Code of Conduct on the Distribution and Use of Pesticides and FAO guidelines on pesticide labeling. Labels must be approved by the national pesticide regulatory authority and include information such as product use category (e.g., professional, restricted, household), directions for use, storage and disposal instructions, supplier identification (local distributor or supplier name, address, and telephone number), and the name and logo of the manufacturer. The release date of the product and shelf life (if less than two years) must also be indicated. Suppliers have responsibilities beyond delivering pesticides, including product stewardship, training, and proper disposal of empty containers. Tender documents should require suppliers to provide evidence of their legal and financial standing, technical and management expertise, long-term viability, and ability to produce products meeting national or WHO specifications. Local suppliers sourcing pesticides from international manufacturers must demonstrate that the products meet the required quality and quantity standards. Delivery schedules and locations must be specified in the tender documents, along with details such as volume, price, Incoterms, and lead time. Safeguards should be included to ensure fair procurement and effective management of the pesticides. Conditions may include ensuring acceptable remaining shelf life at delivery, allowing the procurement entity to examine and sample products, and requiring suppliers to replace or refund costs for non-compliant products. Suppliers may also be required to bear the cost of quality control testing in accredited laboratories. Additional conditions, subject to mutual agreement, may include the collection and proper disposal of empty containers, the return of unused products, provision of protective gear and safety materials, and training in the proper handling and use of pesticides. The tender process must comply with national legal requirements for public procurement and pesticide regulation, ensuring transparency, fairness, and integrity. A tender committee, typically composed of senior officers with expertise in procurement and technical aspects, oversees the process, evaluates bids, and ensures compliance with procurement laws. Members must declare any conflicts of interest to safeguard the committee's integrity. Technical officers evaluating tenders must verify the accuracy of product and supplier information, including compliance with WHO specifications, supported by documentary evidence such as certificates of analysis. Tenders with false or incomplete information should be disqualified. Financial evaluation considers factors such as bid completeness, bidder profile, financial analysis, proven experience, assurance of supply, unit price, and value for money. The technical subcommittee should provide necessary information to ensure the best value for money, particularly for products like indoor residual spraying pesticides.
